rv.q: Eurotrash *is* a good time, and if you find a better time in a theatre this season then it's going to be one hell of a Christmas.
This uproariously funny Young Vic show has absolutely nothing in common with the squalid late-night Channel 4 show of the same name.
Kathryn Hunter and Ben Whishaw excel in this eccentric mother-son Swiss road trip
What you get instead is the strange accomplishment of brilliant streaks of drama in a story with holes.
The bag of make-believe faeces that splashes onto the stage towards the end of the evening turns out to be an all too apt metaphor for what we have had to endure.
Witty and poignant, Eurotrash gets the standing ovation it deserves on press night.
Eurotrash grows into a moving meditation on family, resentment, trauma, and healing.
It’s whirring, wise and wonderful, a gift not just for Christmas but for life.
The energy of the duo is mind-blowing.
Under director Walter Meierjohann’s guidance, the cast and creative team have generated an absurdist dynamic, which constantly surprises, tickles and unsettles.
Whishaw and Turner have the star factor in spades — and together, they show us a great time.
Hunter is impossible to tear your eyes from: cruelly impish, eccentric and brisk, she has a bottomless vault of damaging insults to spew at her son in a rasping, husky voice.

Its ability to surprise and delight through miraculous writing and ingenious direction and the sensational performances from actors at the top of their game barely scratch the surface as to what makes this production so utterly exceptional.
It is an impressive piece of work.
The journey on which the two characters embark is hilarious and ridiculously good fun...
We came to see Whishaw, who's always reliably brilliant on a stage as he is here, but left bowled over by an age-defying performance from the formidable Kathryn Hunter.
'Eurotrash' is a devilishly funny meditation on greed, guilt and reckoning.
And Whishaw and Hunter’s driving stamina and brakeless chemistry make this road-trip comedy far less tyresome (pedestrian, if you prefer) than it could have been.
On those terms it's satisfying because the stars absolutely deliver like you'd hope they would

cn.t: Mostly glowing reviews for this Young Vic adaptation, with Hunter and Whishaw's chemistry earning near-universal praise. One dissenting critic calls it self-indulgent, but most find it a deliriously funny, darkly moving Christmas treat.
